title: What makes a sentence
goal: Say complete sentences with a subject and a verb
intro: A sentence is a group of words that makes complete sense. In English almost every sentence needs two things: someone or something (the subject) and what they do or are (the verb). In Hindi and many Indian languages we often drop the subject, but English doesn’t let you.

examples: The office is near the station.

rules.rule: Every sentence needs a subject, even when it is obvious. Use “it” for weather, time and distance.
examples: It takes ten minutes to walk there.

rules.rule: Use “there is / there are” to say that something exists.
examples: There is a problem with my laptop.

mistakes.why: English needs a subject, so we add “it”.
Add a subject and a verb: it is.

mistakes.wrong: In my office are many people.
mistakes.right: There are many people in my office.
mistakes.why: Use “there are” to say something exists.

ex.y: For weather we use “it” as the subject.
The sentence needs a verb: is based.

ex.q: ___ takes two hours to reach Pune.
ex.y: For time and distance we use “it”.

ex.q: Is very late, let's go home.
ex.fixed: It is very late, let's go home.
ex.y: The sentence has no subject. Add “it”.

ex.q: My phone not working since morning.
ex.fixed: My phone hasn't been working since morning.
ex.y: The sentence needs a verb: hasn’t been working.

ex.q: In this city are many good schools.
ex.fixed: In this city there are many good schools.
ex.y: Use “there are” for things that exist.

ex.q: ___ is a meeting at four o’clock.

ex.a: It is too noisy in here.

ex.q: Make it a full sentence: “Very crowded today.”
ex.y: Add the subject and the verb: It’s very crowded today.

talk: Describe the weather and your street right now in three or four full sentences. Start each sentence with a subject, like “It is…” or “There are…”.
